title: How do you solve a market entry case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete market entry case guide: the four questions, a worked coffee-chain example with market size, share and payback, common mistakes and practice…
hook: Market entry cases ask a yes-or-no question, and the best answers put a number on the prize and compare it with the cost of getting in. Here is the full approach, with a worked example you can follow line by line.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

A new country, customer segment or product category.

The structure

Why this market, and what would success look like, by when?
  • Is the market attractive?
    • Size and growth
    • Typical margins
    • Barriers to entry
  • Can we win?
    • Competitors and their strength
    • What customers need
    • Our edge
  • Will it pay? (compare with payback target)
    • Revenue we can expect
    • Running costs
    • Upfront investment
  • Can we pull it off?
    • Capabilities we lack (decides build, partner or buy)
    • Timing and pilot
    • Key risks

The prize = market size × the share you can win × margin. Compare it with the upfront investment, then say how you would enter.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a UK coffee chain wants to open 40 cafés in Germany's five biggest cities within five years. Should it?

Step 1: size the market. About 10M people live in the target cities. Say 20% buy café coffee in a typical week, about 2 cups each, at €3.50.

  • 10M × 20% = 2M weekly buyers
  • 2M × 2 cups × 52 weeks = 208M cups a year
  • 208M × €3.50 ≈ €730M a year

Step 2: what share can we win? Rivals are strong, so assume 3% by year five: about €22M of revenue.

Step 3: will it pay? At a 15% store margin, profit is about €3.3M a year. Opening 40 cafés at €0.6M each costs €24M upfront. Payback is 24 ÷ 3.3 ≈ 7 years.

Step 4: so what? If the client wants payback within five years, entering alone with 40 cafés does not meet the target.

Recommendation: "The market is large, around €730M, but at a realistic 3% share, 40 company-owned cafés pay back in about seven years, beyond the five-year target. I'd recommend entering through a partner or franchise to cut upfront cost, starting with 10 cafés in one city to test demand before committing further."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Spending ten minutes describing the market and never putting a number on the prize.
  2. Assuming a share without justifying it against competitors.
  3. Forgetting the upfront investment and payback, which is usually what decides the case.
  4. Answering "yes" or "no" without saying how to enter (alone, partner, buy) and how to reduce risk.

Phrases to use

The prize is market size × the share we can win × margin. Let me size each in turn.
Payback of seven years is above the five-year target, so the question becomes how to enter more cheaply.

Practise with these prompts

Should a luxury hotel group launch a budget hotel brand?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Size and growth of budget hotels; Competitors and their returns
  • Economics: Cost to build or convert, room rates, occupancy; Return vs our cost of capital
  • Fit and risk: Can we run low-cost hotels well?; Damage to the luxury brand
  • Cannibalisation: Guests who would trade down from our hotels; Net new profit

Where to start: Economics per hotel: if a single hotel doesn't make money, nothing else matters.

The trap: Forgetting the brand risk and cannibalisation for an existing luxury group.

Should an airline launch a co-branded credit card?

Show a model structure
  • Customer value: Who would use it; Points earned and redeemed
  • Economics: Bank pays us per card and per point; Cost of rewards (seats) and marketing
  • Partner: Which bank, terms, exclusivity; Risk sharing
  • Risks: Brand if the bank treats customers badly; Too many free seats given away

Where to start: Economics: what the bank pays per point vs what a reward seat costs us.

The trap: Treating it as a pure brand decision when it is mainly a points business.

Should an airline launch a daily London–Lagos route?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Demand by segment: business, visiting family, cargo; Seasonality
  • Competition: Rivals' flights, prices, loyalty; Likely response
  • Economics: Revenue per flight vs cost per flight; Aircraft we would take from other routes
  • Risks: Currency, repatriating cash; Airport slots and approvals

Where to start: Profit per flight vs what the aircraft earns elsewhere.

The trap: Forgetting the opportunity cost of the aircraft.

Keep going

  • The framework on its own
  • The quick version: first question and trap
  • More practice prompts in this area

Make entry economics specific to the route chosen

Consider a speciality bakery from one UK city entering a neighbouring city. It could open its own stores, franchise to a local operator or sell packaged products through supermarkets. "Enter the market" is not one decision: the routes have different capital needs, margins, control and speed.

Assume the bakery opens two stores. Each costs £400,000 upfront and expects 250 transactions a day, an £8 average basket and 350 operating days. That is £700,000 annual revenue per store, or £1.4 million across two sites. If food and packaging cost 30% of sales and store labour, rent and local overhead total £400,000 per store, the two stores generate approximately £180,000 annual operating contribution combined, before central overhead, tax, depreciation and financing. Simple payback on the £800,000 opening investment would be about 4.4 years, ignoring ramp-up and working capital.

Now stress-test the assumption that matters most: transactions. If each store draws 200 transactions rather than 250, annual revenue per site falls to £560,000. With the same cost structure, contribution drops sharply. A candidate should not hide this sensitivity behind a precise payback figure. Test footfall, observed conversion rates, competition and the share of customers who would otherwise buy from existing stores.

The recommendation could be a pilot, not a yes-or-no commitment. Lease one site with an exit option, measure repeat purchases and contribution for twelve weeks, and decide whether to roll out. The best entry mode follows from the economics and the client's tolerance for irreversible investment.
